I am 55 years old, finished middle school, and have farmed these 40 mu in Quzhou for 30 years. That is a lot of land for just two people, so I hire a tractor service for rotary tillage and combining, and I hire laborers for cotton picking. I cannot do it all with my own hands.

I put 30 mu into the wheat-maize rotation and keep 10 mu for cotton. The wheat-maize land is my main income. Last year my wheat made about 480 kg per mu and maize about 580 kg. This year I want to reach 500 kg for wheat and 600 kg for maize. For wheat I use an improved variety that I have planted for five years — I know how it behaves here. For maize I use hybrid seed. My neighbor Li tried a new hybrid last year and got 620 kg per mu, so I bought the same bags from the seed dealer. I only change when I see it work in someone else's field first.

For fertilizer, the input dealer talks about NPK balance, and I listen because he knows the products. But I learned from 30 years that nitrogen is what fills the grain. Wheat gets 20 kg nitrogen per mu — I spread compound fertilizer at sowing and top-dress with urea at jointing. Phosphate is 6 kg per mu, potassium 5 kg. Maize gets 18 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphate, 4 kg potassium. Cotton needs more potassium for the bolls, so I give it 18 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphate, and 8 kg potassium. I would rather put a little too much fertilizer than risk a thin harvest. Wasting some fertilizer costs a few hundred yuan; losing a crop costs tens of thousands.

My well gives reliable water. I irrigate wheat 3 times: after sowing to help it settle, at jointing, and at grain filling. Maize gets 2 times: at the big trumpet leaf stage and at silking. Cotton gets 3 times: at planting, at flowering, and when the bolls are filling. The electricity bill for the pump is real money, but with 40 mu I cannot sit and wait for rain.

For chemicals, wheat gets 2 sprays — one herbicide after sowing and one for aphids or rust if they show up. Maize gets 2 sprays. Cotton is the most trouble, needing 4 sprays minimum for bollworm, aphids, and mites. If the weather stays wet and humid, I might need a fifth spray.

For tillage, I rotary till before wheat sowing. For maize, I plant no-till right behind the combine — this saves time between the two crops, and the wheat stubble mulch helps keep moisture in the soil. For cotton, I deep plough because the taproots need loose soil down deep.

I do not experiment much. I watch what Li and Old Wang do. If they try something new and it works, I copy it the next year. Change is risky. But on 40 mu, I also have to think about getting the work done fast, so machines and hired help are just part of the business.
